summary: Young learners (ages 5–7) build a small set of vivid, true penguin facts: penguins are birds whose wings became flippers, so they cannot fly but swim superbly; almost all wild penguins live in the southern half of the world (Antarctica and southern coasts and islands), not the North Pole; Emperor penguins are the largest penguin and survive winter by huddling to share warmth and rotating who stands on the cold outside edge; and an Emperor penguin's single egg is kept warm balanced on a parent's feet under a warm belly flap (brood pouch) instead of in a nest (many other kinds of penguin do use nests or burrows). In Emperor penguins the mother passes the egg to the father, who holds it through the coldest winter; the parents then take turns caring for the chick. Core activities use a labelled penguin scene (picture-first, including a size line-up for 'biggest'), an embodied huddle/waddle enactment, a balance-the-egg task, and optional check and conversation companions.
misconceptions: Penguins live at the North Pole (or with polar bears) — they live in the south, and polar bears are in the north
Penguins aren't birds because they can't fly — they are birds; their wings are flippers for swimming
Penguins are always freezing and alone — they huddle together and take turns to share warmth
The mother penguin sits on the egg in a nest — in Emperors the father balances the egg on his feet, off the ice
All penguins live on ice/snow — many penguin species live in warmer southern places, not only Antarctica

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal labelled penguin scene
steps: Meet a big Emperor penguin standing on Antarctic ice in a labelled picture.
See the tall Emperor penguin lined up next to a child for size — Emperor penguins are the biggest penguins.
Tap its wing to reveal: 'These are flippers — penguins are birds that swim, not fly.'
Tap its feet to see a warm belly flap folding down over a single egg balanced on top (no nest — the egg stays off the ice).
Tap the crowd behind it to zoom into a tight huddle, with arrows showing penguins shuffling from the freezing outside edge into the cosy middle and back out.
Lift a flap answering 'How do they stay warm in the coldest place on Earth?' to see the huddle sharing heat and taking turns.
Find Antarctica at the bottom of a globe so penguins stay firmly in the south.
activities.insight: Penguins are birds whose wings are swimming flippers (not flying wings) and they live in the south; Emperor penguins are the biggest, and they survive winter by huddling as a team and keeping the egg off the ice on a parent's feet.

activities.title: Be the huddle, do the waddle
steps: Waddle like a penguin across the room, then stop and huddle close with others (or with soft toys).
Take turns being on the cold outside edge, then shuffle into the warm middle so everyone gets a warm turn.
Say aloud why the huddle keeps everyone warmer than standing alone.
Balance a pretend 'egg' (beanbag/ball) on your feet and shuffle without dropping it onto the 'ice' — the egg has no nest, so it must stay on the feet.
activities.insight: Sharing warmth and taking turns on the cold edge is a team survival behaviour; keeping the egg on the feet (not in a nest) keeps it off the freezing ground.

activities.title: Friend who's half right — correct it
steps: Listen to a friend's claim: 'Penguins live up at the North Pole near the polar bears, and they're birds so of course they can fly.'
Say what is wrong and fix it.
Answer: if a penguin is a bird that can't fly, what is it brilliant at instead?
Explain how Emperor penguins survive the freezing winter.
activities.insight: A learner who holds the concept relocates penguins to the south, says they are birds that swim rather than fly, and explains huddling and egg-on-feet.

activities.title: Chat with an Emperor penguin
steps: Talk with a friendly Emperor penguin about life in the cold.
Ask how it keeps its egg warm and what it does in the winter wind.
Ask why it can't fly and what its wings do instead.
Retell one fact you learned to a grown-up or friend.
activities.insight: Penguins are birds that swim with flipper-wings; Emperor penguins huddle to share warmth and balance their egg on the feet (no nest) under a warm flap.

checkQuestion: Here's a penguin. A friend says 'penguins live up at the North Pole near the polar bears, and they're birds so of course they can fly.' What would you correct, and if a penguin is a bird that can't fly, what is it brilliant at instead — and how do Emperor penguins survive the freezing winter?
checkAnswer: Two corrections: penguins live in the far SOUTH (Antarctic and southern lands), not the North Pole, so they're nowhere near polar bears; and even though they are birds, penguins CANNOT fly — but they are superb SWIMMERS, using their wings like flippers underwater. Emperor penguins (the biggest) survive winter by huddling together in a big group to share warmth, and parents keep the egg warm balanced on their feet, off the ice.
